The measurement of tibiotalar overlap. The lateral tibial edge is superimposed on the talar edge. Three lines are drawn: (I) the line parallel to the tibial articular surface, (II) the line parallel to the talar articular surface, and (III) the line parallel to the tibial weight-bearing ridge. The location of the highest point of the tibial articular surface (point A), talar articular surface (point B), and tibial weight-bearing ridge (point C) is determined. The tibiotalar overlap angle is the angle between the line connecting point A and point B (Line AB) and line III (Line CD). The tibial articular surface coverage is the percentage of the area of the tibial articular surface (attached to the tibial plateau) covered by the tibial plateau weight-bearing ridge (the line connecting point C and point B).

A 2-day-old female infant with a birth weight of 2,700 grams was admitted to the tertiary pediatric care center because of respiratory distress syndrome. On admission, a bedside ultrasound examination showed pleural effusion and atelectasis of the right lung. The infant was initially diagnosed with bacterial pneumonia and treated with intravenous antibiotics. However, the clinical status did not improve, and the right lung atelectasis progressed and pleural effusion worsened. The lung ultrasound was repeated after 3 days of treatment, and the results showed the rapid development of atelectasis and pleural effusion in the right lung, which suggested the presence of a pulmonary embolism. Pulmonary artery spiral CT was performed, which showed that the main pulmonary artery was severely narrowed, and a large amount of thrombus was in the proximal right pulmonary artery, which was consistent with the results of lung ultrasound. The patient was then treated with a pulmonary embolism with targeted therapy.

Ultrasound image of the sternocostaljoints. The arrow shows the needle trajectory to visualize the axillary artery (AxA) and sternocostaljoints. The needle is advanced into the axillary artery until it is surrounded by the axillary artery and the sternocostaljoints are visualized. The axillary artery is identified by its hypoechoic mural layers and hyperechoic lumen. The sternocostaljoints are seen as two circular hyperechoic structures. The axillary vein (v) is identified by the hyperechoic blood in the vessel. The muscle (M) and rib (R) are identified by their hypoechoic texture. The sternocostaljoints are located between the axillary artery and the sternal border of the fifth rib. The manubrium (B) and the clavicular bone (CB) are identified by their hyperechoic texture. Sagittal CT image of a dog's cervical spine. The figure shows the measurements of the facet angle (FA) and the width of a facet joint (FW). To measure the FA, a line is drawn through the most caudal points of the articular surface of the vertebral bodies and a second line is drawn through the most caudal points of the cranial articular surfaces of the respective adjacent vertebral bodies. The angle between these two lines is the FA. To measure the FFW, a line is drawn through the most cranial and caudal points of the articular surfaces of a facet joint (in this case a right caudal cranial facet joint) and a perpendicular line is drawn through the midpoint of this line.

Measurement of the femoral rotational angle. The femoral rotational angle is formed by the intersection of the anatomical axis of the femur (red) and the mechanical axis of the tibia (green) through the center of the tibial spines. The anatomical axis of the femur is defined by the perpendicular intersection of the medial and lateral cortex of the femur with the tibial plateau. The mechanical axis of the tibia is defined by the midpoint between the anterior and posterior cortical margins of the tibial plateau and the midpoint between the anterior and posterior cortical margins of the tibial medial and lateral aspects. The femoral rotational angle is defined as the angle formed by femoral anatomical and mechanical axes.

Ultrasound image of the suprasternal notch. The image is acquired from the midline view of the neck at the suprasternal notch level. This view shows the thyroid cartilage, anterior and lateral tracheal walls, the esophagus, and the carotid artery in the long axis. The thyroid cartilage is hyperechoic and composed of two distinct parts: the anterior and posterior portions. The thyroid cartilage is the most anterior and hyperechoic structure that forms the anterior border of the cervical esophagus and trachea. The left and right thyroid cartilage borders are usually rounded and smooth. The anterior border of the thyroid cartilage forms a smooth and regular border of the long cervical esophagus. The thyroid cartilage forms a C-shaped structure in the long view of the neck. The esophagus forms a loop-shaped structure in the long view of the neck. The thyroid cartilage forms the anterior border of the long cervical esophagus. The esophagus forms the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage. The carotid artery is usually hyperechoic and has a smooth border and is usually located just lateral to the esophagus.

Example of a properly processed dataset. The image is a 51 y/o female with degenerative disc disease and spinal stenosis. The axial (e-h) and sagittal (a-d) images were processed using ImageJ to include the intervertebral disc space and the spinous process, the latter included only if present in the image. The intervertebral disc space was divided into anterior, middle and posterior zones. The interspinous distance was used to divide the lumbar spine into 3 segments per plane: L4/5 (lower), L5/S1 (middle), and S2/S3 (upper). Each zone, in the interspinous plane, was then divided into anterior, middle and posterior segments with respect to the spinous process. Spinal cord/conus medullaris were included in the sagittal images. The images also demonstrate the use of contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) for image enhancement.

Ultrasound image in a patient with mature cystic teratoma. The presence of hyperechoic lines (cuneiform or 'spicules') is pathognomonic for MCN [56]. MCN is associated with a poor outcome in ovarian cancer [57]. Therefore, the identification of these lines allows for the inclusion of ovarian tumors with this histology in ovarian cancer-specific high-risk stratification and targeted treatment (e.g., hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy, additional high-dose chemotherapy, or ovarian tissue resection) [58,59]. In our study, MCN was present in 100% of the ovarian tumors with ovarian cancer. This is in line with the results of PMP, where MCN was also present in 100% of the ovarian tumors.

Image of a rat heart showing a 16-hour [68Ga]PSMA-6B4 PET-MRI acquisition. The image is multi-planar reformatted and displayed in a coronal view. As the contrast agent is injected directly into the venous system, PSMA-6B4 is delivered to the heart via a single bolus. This results in a rapid and uniform uptake, as shown in this image. During the subsequent imaging period, the PSMA-6B4 contrast agent is slowly released into the heart tissue. This veno-arterial distribution allows for venography of the heart, providing information about cardiac contractility. When the contrast agent has been released, the PSMA-6B4 signal is still high, but now also high in the arterial vessels, providing an additional contrast agent overlay to the images

Dehiscence at the base of the articular surface of the os acromiale (OA). The diameter of this ossicle was measured on a 2D CT cross-section that matched the size of the largest possible ossicle found on sagittal CT images (3 mm) to determine how much of the ossicle was included in the 3D volume. The distance between the articular surface and the outer cortical bone of the ossicle was measured on the sagittal CT planes where the ossicle was seen to be most circular. This value was then used to calculate a 3D-based percentage de-hiscence. Definition of the relative organ dose (ROD) in the prostate gland. The prostate gland is divided into three relative organ dose–convoluted zones: the central core (Zone-intra), the peripheral zone (Zone-peri), and the normo-prostatic zone (Zone-norm). For prostate cancer, a prescription dose of 120 Gy is usually given to the prostate gland. The prostate gland is further divided according to the relative organ dose into three zones: the central core (Zone-intra) between 45%–100% of the organ dose, the peripheral zone (Zone-peri) between 20%–45% of the organ dose, and the normo-prostatic zone (Zone-norm) between 0%–20% of the organ dose.

A 30-year-old woman with right sacroiliitis (arrows). The anteroposterior pelvis radiograph showed sclerosis and irregularities of the right sacroiliac joint margins, which were considered as right sacroiliitis. The right sacroiliac joint was not involved in the inflammatory arthritis criteria (diagnostic criteria of the inflammatory type of arthritis [21]). We measured the width of the right joint space and articular surfaces. We also measured the pre- and post- sacro-iliac joint erosions width. The right area of erosions width was measured to be 6.83 mm2. We defined erosions width as erosions width/joint space width. The right erosions width/joint space width ratio was 0.84. The patient was diagnosed with grade 2 erosive sacroiliitis according to the modified NY criteria [22].

Postoperative lateral whole-leg radiograph, with the anatomic axes (bold lines) and the corresponding mechanical axes (dotted lines) illustrated. The anatomic joint axis (mJFA) is the anatomic joint center, the center of rotation of the femoral shaft, and the center of the ankle joint. Mechanical hip and knee axes were defined as the anatomical axes of the femoral shaft and tibia, respectively. Mechanical joint axes were defined as the center of rotation of the femoral shaft, the center of the knee joint, and the center of rotation of the tibia. Mechanical hip (mHFA), mechanical knee (mKFA), and mechanical distal tibia angles (mDTA), mechanical lateral distal femoral angle (mLDFA), mechanical lateral proximal tibia angle (mLPTA), and anterior mechanical leg parameters (AM) were calculated according to the following equations (as described in Fig. 3): Mechanical HFA = anatomic JFA + mechanical HFA; mechanical KFA = anatomic JFA + mechanical KFA; mDTA = anatomic DTA + mDTA; mechanical LDFA = anatomic LDFA + mLDFA; mechanical LPFA = anatomic JFA + mechanical LPFA; and AM = (mLDFA + mDTA)/2 + mKFA. Mechanical LPFA = anatomic JFA + mechanical LPFA; and AM = (mLDFA + mDTA)/2 + mKFA

Example image of Nodular type lung cancer in a female, 68 years old. Axial CT image shows a dominant nodule (8.0 mm) in the left upper lobe. Pathological diagnosis confirmed stage IA, G2, T1N0M0 lung cancer. The lesion was classified as the first category based on the scoring system. Scored 3 points for the lesion being solid, 3 points for being spiculated, 2 points for being a groundglass opacity, 2 points for being a nodule, and 0 points for being peripherally located. Therefore, the total score was 9 points and the risk score was classified as TR5. The final risk score was TR5.

The figure shows a 70-year-old female patient who underwent PCNL for left nephrocalcinosis. The arrow indicates the left renal artery, the arrowhead indicates the left ureteral stump, and the dashed circle represents the stone burden. The patient underwent PCNL 2 years ago. The axial plane of the CT image obtained during PCNL shows the left renal artery located in the retroaortic space, implying a retroaortic course. The left ureteral stump was placed posterior to the left renal artery, implying a posterolateral contact with the left renal artery. The local clinic determined the angle between the left renal artery and the left ureteral stump to be 7°, which is within the normal range (0°–15°). However, PCNL for left nephrocalcinosis may be considered a contraindication to PCNL for right nephrocalcinosis because of the potential for ureteral stump migration. Further, the patient experienced ureteral stump migration after PCNL for left nephrocalcinosis. Thus, the patient was determined to have a contraindication to PCNL for right nephrocalcinosis based on this CT image

MRI of the lumbar spine.MRI axial view of the lumbar spine at the L5-S1 level demonstrating the anterior hypogastric complex (AH) and posterior free lumbar nerve (PF). Anterior to the quadratus lumborum (QL) and posterior to the Psoas major (PM), the anterior hypogastric complex (AH) contains the lumbar sympathetic plexus and the anterior hypogastric nerve. The QL muscle forms the anterior border of the complex, the PM forms the posterior border, and the quadratus lumborum fascia forms the roof of the complex. The posterior free lumbar nerve originates from the root of the left lumbar (LHP) and travels over the lateral margin of the PMPL to the front of the left PM from where it travels over the lateral border of the QL to the anterior hypogastric complex. This nerve complex is also known as the Adamkiewicz nerve.

A representative anteroposterior radiograph of the lumbar spine was used for measuring the intervertebral disc height, segmental lordosis, segmental kyphosis, and pedicle width. The intervertebral disc height (green line), segmental lordosis (yellow line), segmental kyphosis (orange line), pedicle width (red line), and spinopelvic angle (blue line) were measured using ImageJ software, which was based on the pre-set drawing tool. A: the lower endplate of the upper vertebral body, the maximal distance from the lower endplate to the upper endplate on the anteroposterior direction of the vertebral body. B: the maximal distance of the upper endplate of the lower vertebral body to the lower endplate of the upper vertebral body on the anteroposterior direction of the vertebral body. Disc height=B/A. C: the upper endplate of the lower vertebral body, the maximal distance from the upper endplate to the lower endplate on the anteroposterior direction. D: the midpoint of the pedicle of the upper vertebral body, the greatest distance from the midpoint to the pedicle on the anteroposterior direction. The pedicle width=D/2. E: the lower endplate of the lower vertebral body, the greatest distance from the lower endplate to the upper endplate on the anteroposterior direction of the vertebral body. F: the upper endplate of the upper vertebral body, the greatest distance from the upper endplate to the lower endplate on the anteroposterior direction of the vertebral body. Segmental kyphosis=a+b+c+d+e/2. Segmental lordosis=f/2. Disc height=b/a.

Results are shown for the N400 contrast (FDR>85). The functional connectivity map that was used for the correlation analysis with the N400 task results is displayed in color. We considered both the strength of the functional connectivity (the strength of the connection is determined by average absolute values of the fMRI activation overlap between the condition of interest and the control condition) and its orientation (the direction represents the functional connectivity are determined by the principal eigenvectors of the connectivity matrix). In this example, we show the positive and negative values of functional connectivity strength (yellow and blue colors, respectively). The yellow line indicates the approximate location of the superior temporal gyrus where the N400 contrast (FDR>85) was most prominent. We then examined the functional connectivity strength and its orientation for the N400 contrast (FDR>85) as a function of both location (along the superior temporal gyrus, from posterior to anterior, indicated by the yellow line; see Figure 5) and as a function of functional connectivity strength and its orientation for the N400 contrast (FDR>85).

The pulmonary veins course in the RA and pass through the interatrial septum into the LA. The right atrial and right ventricular margins are obscured by a heterogeneous mass in RA. The mass extends into the LA through a patent foramen ovale (PFO). The mass extends into the RV through an atrial septal defect (ASD). The mass extends into the aorta through an aortopulmonary collateral vessel (APCV). The mass extends into the LV through an interatrial communication. The mass extends into the main pulmonary artery through an intracavitary lesion in the PA. The mass extends into the RV through an intracavitary lesion in the RV. Radiographic appearance of a severe SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia with diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities. The 'Ground-glass sign' is characterised by a more or less diffuse, bilateral presence of a fine reticular pattern superimposed with an increased translucency of the lung parenchyma. This pattern is frequently associated with bilateral pleural effusions. The 2nd–9th double ratio (2-9DR) is calculated as the mean of the distances between the 2nd and 9th posterior ribs and the 2nd and 9th posterior end plates of the first and second lumbar vertebrae, divided by the length of the transverse axis of the chest. The 2-9DR was 0.413 and 0.436 cm in our patient. In the presence of ground-glass opacities, an increased 2-9DR (<0.5 cm) is associated with a negative outcome [4].

A 10-year-old boy with a three-month history of right hip pain. Findings: Pelvic radiograph shows sclerosis and lucency with subchondral bone plate collapse in bilateral femoral capital epiphyses (arrows). The differential diagnosis includes osteonecrosis of the capital femoral epiphysis and atypical femoral fractures. The patient was referred to an orthopedic oncologist for possible Perthes disease and/or atypical femoral fractures. The initial workup included a bone scan which was negative for osteonecrosis. Ankle x-rays were also negative. After two-months of medical management with increased physical therapy, the patient's pain was largely resolved. At three-month follow-up, the patient had a negative bone scan and was able to return to full sports activities. The patient was subsequently referred for further hip evaluation. The differential diagnosis was further expanded to include non-obstructive JIA, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis and AVN. The patient was started on IV antibiotics and hip aspiration was performed which revealed a negative culture. Further imaging including an MRI was performed.
